## Example (multi-paragraph, reproducible): How to recognize and avoid pyramid-scheme swindles

A pyramid scheme is a setup where participants make money primarily by recruiting new participants, not by selling a legitimate product or service to real customers. Because rewards depend on continual recruitment, the scheme mathematically collapses: most people near the bottom lose money.

Common warning signs include: promises of high or “guaranteed” returns, pressure to “get in early,” earnings that depend more on recruiting than on sales to outsiders, unclear or overpriced products used as a cover, and complicated commission structures that are hard to explain plainly. Another red flag is when you’re asked to pay an upfront “starter kit” or “membership fee” and are told you’ll earn it back by bringing in others who do the same.

If you suspect a scheme, take practical steps: ask for audited financials and clear revenue breakdowns; verify whether there’s real demand from non-participants; search for enforcement actions or complaints; and consult your local consumer-protection agency or financial regulator. If a friend tries to recruit you, you can respond neutrally: “I’m not comfortable with anything that pays primarily for recruitment. Can you show how most participants earn from retail sales to non-members?”

If you’ve already paid money, document everything (messages, contracts, receipts), stop sending additional funds, and report it to the relevant authorities in your country. Many regions have dedicated fraud reporting portals, and early reporting can help others avoid being swindled.
